source.title: Objective drives the consistency of representational similarity across datasets
source.authors: Laure Ciernik; L. Linhardt; Marco Morik; Jonas Dippel; S. Kornblith; Lukas Muttenthaler

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how representational similarity relationships vary across datasets and training objectives, and argues that this dataset dependence qualifies claims of universal convergence. It does not reproduce the original scale-based method.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes 64 vision models across 23 datasets. Rows record its measured cross-dataset similarity consistency, its metric comparisons, and explicit statements about objective, model, and dataset effects. Results cited from other studies are not included. Individual similarity matrices and detailed dataset-pair results shown only in figures are not exhaustively transcribed.
record.test_reason: The study measures how pairwise CKA/RSA similarities among 64 vision models change with the evaluation dataset and the similarity metric. It argues explicitly that Platonic-style convergence claims depend on the stimuli used. This bears directly on V6. Through objective-driven clustering of similarity it also bears on V7's claim that objectives shape alignment. It runs no scale trajectory, cross-modal, seed, mapping or feature-universality test.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that pairwise similarities rarely transfer across datasets and depend on both training objective and dataset structure or domain. SSL models' relative similarities transfer best. Image-text training yields the most similar representation spaces. Architecture and size matter little. The similarity–performance link is dataset-dependent, so whether the Platonic hypothesis holds depends on the dataset.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures linear CKA similarities for many vision-model pairs on multiple datasets, then correlates their relative similarity values across dataset pairs. It also compares RBF CKA and RSA Spearman; this is not the original scale-based alignment test.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with evaluation dataset and dataset domain, training objective, similarity metric, and RBF bandwidth. The paper also reports that local RBF CKA is more sensitive to stimulus sampling than linear CKA.

fits_no_version.finding: Pairwise CKA similarity correlates negatively with the pairwise top-1 performance gap, and the strength is dataset-dependent. Examples: ImageNet-1k r=-0.31, Flowers -0.76, Pets -0.82, Diabetic Retinopathy -0.40, DTD -0.69. The authors say the Platonic claim's validity depends on the dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How strongly representational similarity tracks performance differences depends on the evaluation dataset: strong for single-domain data, weak for multi-domain data such as ImageNet.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised CNNs trained on Places365 have more consistent cross-dataset similarities than the same architectures trained on ImageNet-1k. The authors caution this may reflect specialized solutions rather than convergence on reality (Appx. I, Fig. 20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrower training domains make the relative similarity structure among models more stable across evaluation datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: There is no significant consistency difference between CNNs and transformers. Same-size groups are more consistent than mixed-size groups, but less markedly than the objective effect (§4.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and model size matter little for how well relative representational similarities transfer across datasets.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267 (2025)
record.problems: The 64-model set has confounded attributes: for example, some training-data categories overlap strongly with objectives. The authors note that sample choice affects local CKA more than linear CKA. The main analyses report distributions and selected figures rather than uncertainty intervals for most category comparisons. Performance is evaluated with linear probes, not as a scale trajectory.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports many dataset-pair/objective-specific values in Fig. 6 and Figs. 16–20, plus individual dataset performance-gap correlations in Figs. 21–22. These were not exhaustively transcribed; the aggregate statements and selected explicit results relevant to the tested versions were retained.

untested.parts: No test of whether cross-model alignment rises with model size or capability. The similarity vs performance-gap analysis is a different construct.
Only image encoders are compared; there is no vision–language paired-data alignment.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
Mutual nearest-neighbour metrics and k settings are not tested. Absolute convergence levels are reported only in figures, not as a convergence trend.
No test of plateauing or of how complete alignment is. No test of shared training data as a cause, nor of a 'common model of reality'.

missing.what: Absolute pairwise CKA values vary across datasets (std matrix). Mean similarity vs std follows an inverse U, with mid-range similarities most variable. Mean similarity agrees across metrics (r=0.85 RBF σ=0.2 vs linear; 0.90 RSA vs linear).
Under local RBF CKA σ=0.2, the ordering flips relative to linear CKA: supervised pairs are more consistent than image-text pairs, and IN21k pairs more consistent than IN1k pairs.
Natural vs non-natural (out-of-distribution) evaluation data. Image-text vs supervised consistency has a lower median and higher variance on natural datasets; the objective effect persists.
Bootstrap stability: RBF CKA σ=0.2 values vary more across 500 resampled ImageNet subsets than linear CKA does, so local metrics are more stimulus-sensitive.
t-SNE of similarity matrices clusters by training objective, not by architecture or size. Image-text models form the most mutually similar group.
Anchor-model analysis controlling architecture and size. SSL sets give the highest, least variable consistency against every anchor; image-text anchors correlate weakly with supervised models.
Per-dataset correlations between similarity and performance gap for all 23 datasets. The fits_no_version rows r20–r23 the record referenced do not exist.

record.verdict_notes: The central measure is the cross-dataset Pearson correlation of pairwise similarity vectors, i.e. how stable relative similarity is. It is not convergence level or its trend. V6 verdicts rest on dependence of measured similarity on inputs and metric, not on convergence vanishing. The record's states for r2–r10 were graded as 'consistency' (high r = observed), which inverts V6's direction; they are regraded. Values for r11, r12 and r14 were misassigned in the record and corrected using the text's ordering of correlation strengths. None of the original sources is this study, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether alignment between independently trained models rises as model size or capability increases. It does compare representation similarity with pairwise performance gaps, recorded under fits_no_version.
Image-text models are included, but the study does not compare vision and language representations of paired images and captions or test whether their alignment rises with performance.
The study does not test convergence across random seeds of the same architecture.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test is performed.
The study does not identify recurring interpretable features or circuits.

The study tests dependence on input datasets and similarity metrics, including RBF bandwidth choices, but does not test nearest-neighbour count settings or a systematic out-of-distribution intervention.

The study reports objective- and dataset-dependent similarity patterns. It does not test convergence trajectories with scale, prove that shared objectives cause similarity, or establish whether models converge to a common model of reality.

rows.subject: Model groups by training objective (64 vision models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-dataset consistency of relative pairwise model similarities across training objectives
rows.measure: Relative pairwise similarity consistency across datasets
rows.value: Self-supervised models show the highest consistency; image-text models generally show high similarities; supervised models show the weakest consistency, especially against image-text models.
rows.note: The authors identify training objective as the primary factor in similarity consistency; architecture and model attributes are not fully independent in the model set.
rows.check: This is about how consistent relative similarity is across datasets, not about alignment being explained by objectives, so the V7 link is removed. Dataset dependence is strong for supervised and image-text-vs-supervised pairs and weak for SSL, so the state is partial.

rows.subject: Model groups by architecture and model size (64 vision models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-dataset consistency across architecture and size categories
rows.measure: Relative pairwise similarity consistency across datasets
rows.value: No significant difference in consistency between transformers and convolutional networks; same-size model groups show higher consistency than different-size groups, but size has a less pronounced effect than training objective.
rows.note: This is a result about transferability of similarity relationships, not a test of whether larger models become more aligned.
rows.check: Architecture and model-size effects on consistency concern neither metric/input choice (V6) nor a scale-convergence trajectory (V1). The row notes itself that it is not a test of alignment rising with size.
